c.tagline: City of Lakes where Mississippi mills meet Prince, parks, and prairie winters.

taxi.fareNote: Cabs are metered but scarce on the street; most visitors book Uber or Lyft, which are widely available.

emergency.note: 911 is the single emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Property crime and caution around parts of downtown/transit at night

hood_desc: A former warehouse district turned Minneapolis's most stylish neighborhood, packed with converted-loft boutiques, chef-driven restaurants, craft breweries, and riverside walking paths; ideal for design-minded visitors who want to eat and shop well.

The walkable core along the Mississippi riverfront, home to the historic flour mills, the Guthrie Theater, the Stone Arch Bridge, and the climate-controlled skyway network; the most convenient base for first-timers.

A lively lakeside district beside Bde Maka Ska and Lake of the Isles, full of bars, patios, indie shops, and cyclists; suits younger travelers who want nightlife and the Chain of Lakes on the doorstep.
The old-world 'Nordeast' arts district of galleries, artist studios, taprooms, and classic supper clubs; a favorite for creative types and beer lovers wanting a laid-back, local scene.

The compact student quarter beside the University of Minnesota, dense with cheap eats, coffee shops, and record stores steeped in Bob Dylan lore; good for budget travelers wanting a youthful, energetic vibe.

transit.pay: Tap a Go-To card or a contactless bank card or phone at light-rail platform validators and on buses. A single ride is $2.00 off-peak and $2.50 during rush hours, good for 2.5 hours of transfers. Go-To cards are reloadable and sold at stations and retailers.
transit.hours: Light rail runs roughly 4am to 2am; many bus routes run early morning to around midnight, with a few 24-hour and Owl routes.

train: Saint Paul Union Depot (Amtrak Empire Builder)

tip.r: ~15-20% is standard at restaurants; round up for taxis and tip $1-2 per drink at bars.

food.name: Juicy Lucy
food.desc: The city's own burger: two thin patties sealed around molten American cheese, so the first bite spurts hot cheese. Let it cool a minute.

places.name: Matt's Bar and Grill
places.note: Dive bar serving the Jucy Lucy since the 1950s and still the benchmark version.

places.name: 5-8 Club
places.note: The other half of the long-running rivalry over who invented the stuffed burger.

places.name: Blue Door Pub
places.note: Modern take with stuffed Blucy variations, blue cheese and garlic among them.

food.name: Hotdish
food.desc: Minnesota's one-pan casserole: ground beef, vegetables and creamy soup base under a crown of tater tots, baked until the top goes golden.

places.name: Hazel's Northeast
places.note: Big-portion neighbourhood kitchen that runs tater tot hotdish among its Minnesotan comfort plates.

places.name: Hell's Kitchen
places.note: Downtown basement institution built on Minnesota comfort cooking.

places.name: Minnesota State Fair
places.area: Falcon Heights (late Aug to Labor Day)
places.note: Hotdish in every guise across the food halls if you are here in season.

food.name: Walleye
food.desc: The state fish, usually pan-fried or beer-battered in a sandwich with tartar sauce. Sweet, flaky and a fixture on nearly every Minnesota menu.

places.name: Tavern on Grand
places.note: Northwoods-style tavern that built its name on walleye, fried or sauteed.

places.name: Gluek's Restaurant and Bar
places.note: Historic downtown bar and restaurant with a long-standing walleye plate.

places.name: Sea Salt Eatery
places.note: Park-side seafood shack; walleye sandwiches eaten at picnic tables by the falls.

food.name: Lefse and Scandinavian pastries
food.desc: Soft potato flatbread rolled with butter and sugar, plus the cardamom buns, almond cake and open sandwiches of the city's Nordic heritage.

places.name: FIKA at the American Swedish Institute
places.note: Cafe inside the Swedish Institute mansion doing modern Nordic plates and pastries.

places.name: Ingebretsen's Nordic Marketplace
places.note: Century-old Norwegian grocery and meat counter, the go-to for lefse and lutefisk.

places.name: Rustica Bakery
places.note: Cardamom buns and Scandinavian-leaning pastries baked fresh each morning.

food.name: Somali sambusa
food.desc: Crisp fried triangles stuffed with spiced beef or lentils, eaten with fiery green basbaas sauce. A staple of the largest Somali community in the US.

places.name: Afro Deli
places.note: Popular East African counter serving sambusas, suqaar and rice plates all day.

places.name: Safari Restaurant
places.note: Long-established Somali dining room for goat, camel and pyramid-sized rice platters.

places.name: Karmel Mall food court
places.note: Somali mall where small kitchens sell sambusa, shaah and fresh flatbread.

food.name: Wild rice
food.desc: Manoomin, the hand-harvested lake grain sacred to the Ojibwe, turned into creamy wild rice soup, porridge or a side for game and fish.

places.name: Owamni
places.area: Mill District, by St Anthony Falls
places.note: Award-winning Indigenous kitchen cooking pre-colonial ingredients including manoomin.

places.name: Hell's Kitchen
places.note: Famous for mahnomin porridge, wild rice cooked with cream, berries and hazelnuts.

places.name: Birchwood Cafe
places.note: Farm-to-table neighbourhood cafe that works wild rice into soups and bowls.

food.name: Minnesota craft beer
food.desc: A dense brewery scene of taprooms pouring hoppy ales and lagers, plus Grain Belt, the old Nordeast label that is still the local badge of honour.

places.name: Surly Brewing Destination Brewery
places.note: Huge beer hall and beer garden from the brewery that changed Minnesota beer law.

places.name: Indeed Brewing Company
places.note: Taproom at the heart of the Northeast brewery district, easy to walk between.

places.name: Fulton Beer
places.note: Taproom steps from Target Field, packed before Twins games.

food.name: Bloody Mary with a beer snit
food.desc: Upper Midwest brunch ritual: a heavily garnished bloody mary served with a small glass of beer, the snit, on the side as a chaser.

places.name: Hell's Kitchen
places.note: Brunch institution where the bloody mary comes loaded and with the customary snit.

places.name: Psycho Suzi's Motor Lounge
places.note: Tiki bar with a riverside patio and outsized garnished drinks.

places.name: The Lowry
places.note: Reliable all-day diner-bar for weekend brunch cocktails.

landmarks: Stone Arch Bridge
This historic 1883 limestone railroad bridge over the Mississippi offers classic views of St. Anthony Falls and the downtown skyline.
Minneapolis Sculpture Garden
Home to the beloved Spoonbridge and Cherry sculpture, it's one of the most Instagrammed spots in the city.
Foshay Tower
This 1929 Art Deco obelisk-shaped skyscraper was long the tallest building in the Upper Midwest and remains a downtown icon.
Guthrie Theater
Jean Nouvel's striking blue building features the cantilevered 'Endless Bridge' with a dramatic river and skyline view.
IDS Center
Minneapolis's tallest skyscraper features the striking glass-atrium Crystal Court at its base.
Minnehaha Falls
A picturesque 53-foot waterfall in a wooded park, immortalized in Longfellow's poetry and a favorite nature photo spot.
U.S. Bank Stadium
The glass-and-steel home of the Minnesota Vikings has a distinctive angular, ship-like silhouette on the downtown skyline.
Weisman Art Museum
Frank Gehry's undulating stainless-steel facade overlooking the Mississippi is a striking piece of architecture in its own right.
Walker Art Center
A leading contemporary art museum whose modern building and adjoining sculpture garden are a design-lover's favorite.
Basilica of Saint Mary
The first basilica established in the United States, its Beaux-Arts dome is a landmark of the downtown skyline.

train.note: Two Amtrak trains serve the Twin Cities and both use Saint Paul Union Depot rather than a Minneapolis station - the daily Empire Builder between Chicago and Seattle or Portland, and the Borealis, a second daily Chicago to St Paul train introduced in May 2024 that has proved popular and often needs booking ahead. Union Depot is about eleven miles east of downtown Minneapolis, easily reached on Metro Transit's Green Line light rail in around 45 minutes. No train crosses to Canada from Minnesota - the line north to Winnipeg carries freight only. Empire Builder sleepers open 11 months ahead and sell out for summer travel.

bus.note: No through international coach is currently marketed from the Twin Cities, though Jefferson Lines sells connecting itineraries onward into Canada and Mexico via partner carriers. Jefferson Lines (https://www.jeffersonlines.com/) is the regional workhorse, covering 17 states across the Midwest and Plains from Saint Paul Union Depot, alongside Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/) and Megabus (https://us.megabus.com/). Typical times are about seven hours to Chicago, four to Duluth and four to Fargo. Union Depot is a proper staffed terminal with waiting rooms, which makes winter departures much more pleasant.

ferry.note: Minneapolis lies on the upper Mississippi above St Anthony Falls and has no scheduled passenger ferry service; the river here is for locks, barges and paddlewheel excursion boats rather than transport. The lakes within the city carry canoes and pleasure craft only.

half.name: Stillwater
half.blurb: A historic river town near the St. Croix River, about 30 minutes east, known for antique shops and its 1931 lift bridge.

half.name: Red Wing
half.blurb: A Mississippi River town about an hour southeast known for pottery, boot-making, and bluff-top hiking trails.

half.name: Lake Minnetonka
half.blurb: A large lake just west of the city with lakeside towns, boat cruises, and public swimming beaches.

half.name: Wabasha
half.blurb: A small river town about two hours southeast, home to the National Eagle Center and its rescued bald eagles.
